tagline: Hairpin curves climb to a plateau above Colorado River canyon country
intro: Dead Horse Mesa Scenic Byway climbs through hairpin curves before easing onto a plateau of red rock canyon country. Utah’s tourism office lists the 22.5-mile SR-313 among its state scenic byways, highlighting views of the La Sal, Abajo and Henry mountains and the Bookcliffs. For the longer outing into both Dead Horse Point and Canyonlands, Moab’s tourism office recommends at least two hours, with additional time for the parks.

A county road already reached Dead Horse Point by 1969. Utah took over maintenance and assigned SR-313 in 1975, replacing a proposed state route that was never built. After crews rebuilding the Canyonlands access road damaged SR-313, reconstruction began in 1989. The work reduced the maximum grade from 11 percent to 8 percent and leveled the switchbacks to remove blind corners.

Begin at US-191, about nine miles north of Moab, and climb toward the plateau. At about 14.6 miles, the left fork leads to Dead Horse Point. Return to SR-313, then continue toward Canyonlands’ Island in the Sky district and Grand View Point. Island in the Sky is a broad, level mesa between the Colorado and Green rivers; its viewpoints overlook the White Rim sandstone bench, with the rivers farther below.

moments.title: Monitor and Merrimac
moments.text: Two Civil War ship names turn up above Sevenmile Canyon: Monitor and Merrimac. The buttes are visible from Highway 313 after the climb out of the canyon, with Monitor immediately east of Merrimac. Merrimac is a narrow sandstone mass, 1,600 feet long from east to west. Its vertical Entrada Sandstone walls rise 200 feet above a base of the Carmel Formation. The names refer to ironclad steamships that clashed during the American Civil War; the rock formations can be seen on the drive toward either Dead Horse Point or Island in the Sky.
moments.notice: Look for Monitor immediately east of Merrimac beyond the climb out of Sevenmile Canyon.

moments.title: Dead Horse Point
moments.text: Dead Horse Point’s overlook stands 2,000 feet above the Colorado River, facing Canyonlands’ pinnacles and buttes. The state park opened to the public in 1959. Its high-desert plants grow slowly in conditions of scarce water and extreme temperatures. Small leaves with waxy coatings reduce evaporation; Utah juniper, pinyon pine, blackbrush and narrowleaf yucca are among the park’s plants. The park has several overlooks, with East Rim and West Rim trail loops adding other vantage points. The park’s high desert lies at an elevation of 5,900 feet, and includes a visitor center and picnic areas.
moments.notice: The Colorado River lies 2,000 feet below the overlook.

moments.title: Aztec Butte
moments.text: Stone granaries near the top of Aztec Butte held food gathered by Ancestral Puebloan people who traveled to Island in the Sky to hunt and collect seeds. The granaries date to AD 1200–1300. The butte itself is white, cross-bedded Navajo Sandstone, the remains of wind-borne dunes deposited approximately 170 million years ago. From the Upheaval Dome road, a half-mile trail across flat grassland leads to a quarter-mile scramble gaining 200 feet to the top and granaries. The summit lies in Canyonlands’ Island in the Sky district, and runoff from the butte drains toward the Green River.

practical: Dead Horse Point: A state park entrance fee is required to drive to the Dead Horse Point viewpoints. (checked 2026-10-11)
